title: Cranial Nerve XI (The Spinal Accessory Nerve)
subtitle: Localize weakness of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius from cortex to neck, and recognize the jugular foramen and lower cranial nerve syndromes

points.text: The cranial (internal) root comes from the caudal nucleus ambiguus and travels with the vagus to supply pharynx and larynx.
points.quote: The cranial root arises from cells situated in the caudal part of the nucleus ambiguus of the medulla.

points.text: The spinal root is somatotopic: upper cervical segments serve mainly the sternocleidomastoid and C3-C4 serve mainly the trapezius, which explains why the two muscles can be affected separately.
points.quote: cord levels C1 and C2 innervate predominantly the ipsilateral sternocleidomastoid muscle, and levels C3 and C4 innervate primarily the ipsilateral trapezius

points.text: Cranial and spinal roots join and leave the skull together through the jugular foramen, so skull-base lesions rarely spare neighbouring nerves.
points.quote: The cranial and spinal roots unite and exit from the skull through the jugular foramen.

points.text: Corticobulbar input to the trapezius is crossed, so each hemisphere drives the contralateral trapezius.
points.quote: The corticobulbar fibers to the trapezius are crossed, and thus one cerebral hemisphere supplies the contralateral trapezius muscle.

points.text: The sternocleidomastoid pathway is not well defined; it is thought to end mainly in the ipsilateral nuclei, with several alternative routes proposed.
points.quote: The course of the fibers controlling the sternocleidomastoid muscle is unknown, but the fibers are thought to terminate chiefly in the ipsilateral nuclei.

points.text: Sternocleidomastoid fibers run in the brainstem tegmentum and trapezius fibers run ventrally, which allows dissociated brainstem patterns.
points.quote: The corticobulbar fibers to the sternocleidomastoid are located in the brainstem tegmentum, whereas fibers to the trapezius are located in the ventral brainstem

points.text: A ventral pontine lesion can therefore weaken the trapezius supranuclearly while the sternocleidomastoid is spared.
points.quote: Thus, a ventral pontine lesion can cause supranuclear paresis of the trapezius with sparing of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

points.text: Each sternocleidomastoid turns the face to the opposite side, so the right muscle is tested by turning the head to the left against resistance.
points.quote: The right sternocleidomastoid is thus tested by having the patient rotate his or her head to the left against resistance

points.text: The trapezius is tested with a bilateral shoulder shrug against resistance, comparing the two sides by looking and palpating.
points.quote: muscle is tested by having the patient shrug his or her shoulders against resistance and comparing the two sides by observation and palpation.

localizationRules.explanation: Head position at rest is normal; the deficit is weak turning of the head to the opposite side, and on flexion the head drifts toward the unaffected side because the other muscle is unopposed.
localizationRules.quote: There is weakness in turning the head to the opposite side, and when the patient flexes the head, it rotates slightly

localizationRules.explanation: Look for a low shoulder at rest and a displaced, slightly winged scapula; the upper fibers are mainly affected in nerve XI lesions.
localizationRules.quote: The shoulder is lower on the affected side at rest, and the scapula is displaced downward and laterally with its vertebral border slightly winged.

localizationRules.explanation: Bilateral trapezius weakness weakens neck extension (head falls forward), whereas bilateral sternocleidomastoid weakness weakens neck flexion (head tends to fall backward).
localizationRules.quote: Bilateral trapezius paresis results in weakness of neck extension, with the head tending to fall forward when the patient attempts to stand erect.

localizationRules.explanation: With a hemispheric lesion causing contralateral hemiplegia, the trapezius is weak on the hemiplegic side but the weak sternocleidomastoid is on the side of the cerebral lesion, so the head turns away from the hemiplegic side.
localizationRules.quote: the head is turned away from the hemiplegic side, indicating paresis of the sternocleidomastoid muscle on the side opposite the hemiplegia

localizationRules.rule: Geschwind rule for hemiplegia plus sternocleidomastoid paresis
localizationRules.explanation: Compare the side of the weak sternocleidomastoid with the hemiplegic side: if opposite, think hemisphere; if the same side, the lesion is at or below the pons.
localizationRules.quote: hemiplegia associated with ipsilateral (to the hemiplegia) sternocleidomastoid paresis implies a lesion at or below the pontine level

keySyndromes.name: Jugular foramen syndrome (Vernet)
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral trapezius and sternocleidomastoid paresis and atrophy + dysphonia and dysphagia with depressed gag reflex, palatal droop and vocal cord paralysis + loss of taste and depressed sensation over the posterior third of the tongue, soft palate, pharynx and larynx
keySyndromes.clue: Involves IX, X and XI together; adding tongue paralysis (XII) moves the picture to Collet-Sicard.
keySyndromes.quote: The spinal accessory nerve enters the jugular foramen accompanied by cranial nerve IX (glossopharyngeal nerve) and cranial nerve X (vagus nerve).

keySyndromes.name: Collet-Sicard syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Paralysis of the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid (XI) + paralysis of the vocal cord (X) and pharynx (IX) + hemiparalysis of the tongue (XII) + loss of taste on the posterior third of the tongue (IX) + hemianesthesia of the palate, pharynx and larynx (IX, X)
keySyndromes.clue: All four lower cranial nerves IX to XII on one side; all findings are ipsilateral to the lesion, often in the retroparotid space.
keySyndromes.quote: Involvement of all four of the lower cranial nerves (IX through XII) results in the Collet-Sicard

keySyndromes.name: Villaret syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Cranial nerves IX + X + XI + XII + cervical sympathetic chain (ipsilateral Horner syndrome) + occasionally VII
keySyndromes.clue: Like Collet-Sicard but with sympathetic involvement; located in the retroparotid or retropharyngeal space.
keySyndromes.quote: Lesions of the retroparotid or retropharyngeal spaces may cause Villaret syndrome (affecting cranial nerves IX, X, XI, and XII, the sympathetic chain

keySyndromes.name: Trapezius weak, sternocleidomastoid spared
keySyndromes.triad: Weakness of the trapezius on one side + sparing of the sternocleidomastoid
keySyndromes.clue: Points to a ventral brainstem lesion, a lower cervical cord lesion, or a lower spinal accessory root lesion.
keySyndromes.quote: Weakness of the trapezius on one side with sparing of the sternocleidomastoid muscles indicates a ventral brainstem lesion

keySyndromes.name: Sternocleidomastoid weak, trapezius spared
keySyndromes.triad: Weakness of the sternocleidomastoid + trapezius sparing
keySyndromes.clue: Points to a lower brainstem tegmentum lesion or to upper cervical accessory roots.
keySyndromes.quote: Weakness of the sternocleidomastoid with trapezius sparing indicates a lesion of the lower brainstem tegmentum

keySyndromes.name: Nuclear lesions of the accessory nucleus
keySyndromes.triad: Paresis of trapezius and sternocleidomastoid + prominent atrophy + fasciculations
keySyndromes.clue: Rare; suggested by associated medullary or upper cervical cord dysfunction (motor neuron disease, intraparenchymal tumor, syringomyelia).
keySyndromes.quote: These relatively rare lesions result in paresis with prominent atrophy and fasciculations that affect the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles.

boardTraps.text: Dissociated weakness (trapezius weak on one side, sternocleidomastoid weak on the other) indicates an upper motor neuron lesion ipsilateral to the weak sternocleidomastoid and above the oculomotor complex.
boardTraps.quote: Weakness of the trapezius on one side associated with weakness of the sternocleidomastoid on the other (dissociated weakness) indicates an upper motor neuron lesion

boardTraps.text: Medullary lesions affecting corticobulbar fibers weaken head turning toward the lesion, the opposite of the cortical, capsular and high brainstem pattern.
boardTraps.quote: Thus, medullary lesions affecting corticobulbar fibers may result in decreased strength on the head turning toward the lesion

boardTraps.text: Nerve XI lesions do not cause sensory disturbance, so sensory loss in a jugular foramen syndrome has to come from neighbouring nerves such as IX and X.
boardTraps.quote: Because the spinal accessory nerve is a purely motor nerve (except for some proprioceptive afferent fibers), nerve lesions do not result in sensory disturbance.

boardTraps.text: In nerve XI lesions the trapezius weakness affects predominantly the upper fibers, the part not supplied by the cervical plexus.
boardTraps.quote: Unilateral trapezius paresis due to spinal accessory nerve lesions affects predominantly the upper trapezius fibers (the part not supplied by the cervical plexus).

boardTraps.text: A traction injury in the posterior cervical triangle, distal to the sternocleidomastoid, gives isolated trapezius weakness; the nerve is vulnerable to iatrogenic injury there, for example at lymph node biopsy.
boardTraps.quote: With injuries (e.g., traction) in the posterior cervical triangle distal to the sternocleidomastoid muscle, trapezius weakness occurs in isolation

boardTraps.text: Dropped (floppy) head is not a nerve XI sign by default: the book lists many central, neuropathic, neuromuscular junction, myopathic and mechanical causes in Table 13-2.
boardTraps.quote: Weakness of neck extension against gravity with or without involvement of neck flexion has been called the floppy head syndrome
